title: ACCY 6100 — Auditing Seminar
subtitle: Exam 1 Practice Question Bank
source: Modules 1–4, plus the Meridien/Bond independence case study

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: Who was Ivar Kreuger?

choices.text: A US regulator who investigated early securities fraud
A Swedish industrialist who built a global match monopoly financed by investor securities
The founder of the first US public accounting firm
A congressman who authored the Securities Act of 1933

questions.explanation: Kreuger was a Swedish industrialist who built a global match manufacturing/distribution monopoly financed by securities sold to investors, especially in the US.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: What world event set the stage for Kreuger's rise to prominence?

choices.text: The 1929 stock market crash
World War I, which disrupted European economies and created capital demand
The founding of the SEC
World War II

questions.explanation: WWI disrupted European economies and government finances, creating the capital demand Kreuger filled by lending to governments in exchange for match monopolies.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: What did Kreuger's fraud actually involve, per Flesher & Flesher?

choices.text: He embezzled company cash and inventory directly
He promised governments construction services and failed to deliver
He paid dividends from new investor cash and misstated his financials
He forged bank signatures to authorize transfers

questions.explanation: Kreuger paid investors dividends using cash from new investors (Ponzi-like) rather than real earnings, and intentionally misstated his financial statements — not embezzlement or reneging on services.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: Why did Kreuger's scheme ultimately fail?

choices.text: A whistleblower auditor exposed the fraud
The Great Depression cut off his ability to raise new capital
A foreign government seized his monopolies
Congress banned match monopolies directly

questions.explanation: The Great Depression cut off Kreuger's ability to raise new capital to cover the gaps created by his fabricated structure, leading to his 1932 collapse.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: Which act do Flesher & Flesher credit Kreuger's fraud with contributing to?

choices.text: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934
The Securities Act of 1933
The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002
The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977

questions.explanation: Flesher & Flesher credit Kreuger's fraud specifically with contributing to the Securities Act of 1933, not the 1934 Exchange Act or later reforms.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: What is the auditor's fundamental obligation, per the readings?

choices.text: To serve client management and the audit committee
To protect investors
To detect all instances of fraud
To guarantee the accuracy of every disclosure

questions.explanation: The reading frames the auditor's fundamental obligation as investor protection — broader than the AU-C 200 technical objective of reasonable assurance.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: Per AU-C 200, what is the overall objective of an audit?

choices.text: To guarantee the F/S contain no errors
To obtain reasonable assurance the F/S are free of material misstatement and report accordingly
To prepare the F/S on management's behalf
To design the company's internal controls

questions.explanation: AU-C 200 states the auditor's objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance the F/S are free of material misstatement and to report accordingly.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: Reasonable assurance is best described as:

choices.text: A moderate level of assurance
A high level of assurance
Absolute assurance
A guarantee no material misstatements go undetected

questions.explanation: Reasonable assurance is confirmed as a high level of assurance — not moderate, not absolute, and it does not guarantee zero undetected material misstatements.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: Why is absolute assurance not required or achievable in an audit?

choices.text: It is required but auditors simply aren't held to it
It isn't achievable due to inherent limitations like sampling and possible collusion
It was eliminated by SOX in 2002
It only applies to private companies

questions.explanation: Absolute assurance isn't achievable due to inherent limitations — sampling, the nature of evidence, and possible collusion or concealment.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: What amount of assurance does the auditor obtain regarding IMMATERIAL misstatements?

choices.text: The same reasonable assurance as material misstatements
Little to none — the audit targets material misstatements
Absolute assurance, since they're easier to verify
A separate lower-tier opinion just for immaterial items

questions.explanation: Immaterial misstatements wouldn't influence a reasonable user's decisions, so the audit isn't designed to catch them — assurance is calibrated to material items.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: Which of these is genuinely a management responsibility in a public company audit?

choices.text: Selecting the auditor and negotiating engagement terms
Preparing the F/S and maintaining internal controls
Issuing the final audit opinion
Setting PCAOB inspection schedules

questions.explanation: Management prepares the F/S, maintains internal controls, and supplies information; selecting the auditor and negotiating terms is the audit committee's job, not management's.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: What are the two explanations for the origin/demand for auditing discussed in Module 1?

choices.text: Regulatory mandate theory and market efficiency theory
Agency/stewardship theory and the insurance hypothesis
Signaling theory and deterrence theory
Public interest theory and capture theory

questions.explanation: Agency/stewardship theory ties audit demand to monitoring management on owners' behalf; the insurance hypothesis holds investors demand audits partly to have someone to sue for recovery if losses occur.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: An investor invests partly believing that if the audited F/S turn out wrong, she can sue the auditor to recover losses. Which explanation for audit demand is this?

choices.text: Agency/stewardship theory
The insurance hypothesis
The expectations gap
Adverse selection theory

questions.explanation: The insurance hypothesis holds investors demand audits partly because they believe auditors have deep pockets and can be sued to recover losses.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: How do adverse selection and moral hazard differ?

choices.text: Both occur only after capital is committed
Adverse selection is pre-transaction; moral hazard is post-transaction
Both are the same concept, just different names
Adverse selection is post-transaction; moral hazard is pre-transaction

questions.explanation: Adverse selection is pre-transaction information asymmetry (can't tell good firms from bad before investing); moral hazard is post-transaction (unobservable actions after capital is committed).

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: Why doesn't providing financial statements alone solve the adverse selection problem?

choices.text: Because F/S are legally required to be false
Managers have an incentive to misstate what they self-report, so unaudited F/S aren't credible on their own
Because GAAP doesn't cover most transactions
Because investors never read financial statements

questions.explanation: Managers prepare the F/S investors use to judge them, so self-reported statements aren't credible on their own — investors know this and may distrust or avoid unaudited F/S, shrinking the market to low-quality issuers.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: How is adverse selection overcome so lemons markets can be avoided?

choices.text: By requiring all investors to conduct their own audits
Through independent third-party verification that lacks a stake in favorable results
By banning companies from issuing financial statements
Through government price controls on securities

questions.explanation: Independent third-party verification (the audit) adds credibility because the verifier has no stake in favorable results, helping avoid a lemons market.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: What characteristics make third-party information providers/assurers valuable?

choices.text: Low cost and quick turnaround time
Independence, competence, reputation, and accountability
Close personal ties to company management
A financial stake in the company's success

questions.explanation: Valuable third-party assurers are independent/free of conflicts, competent, reputable, and accountable (exposed to liability) — not simply cheap or fast.

questions.module: Module 1: Theory, Purpose, and Origin of Auditing
questions.prompt: Which event prompted the AICPA to create the Committee on Auditing Procedure in 1939, issuing the first formal US auditing standards?

choices.text: The Ivar Kreuger collapse
The McKesson and Robbins audit failure
The Enron collapse
The 1929 stock market crash

questions.explanation: The McKesson & Robbins fraud (inflated inventory/receivables) directly led the AICPA to create the Committee on Auditing Procedure in 1939, issuing the first formal US auditing standards.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: How did audit regulation change between 1980 and 2005, per Kinney?

choices.text: It became less regulated, moving toward pure self-regulation
It shifted from self-regulation to independent government-mandated PCAOB oversight
It remained essentially unchanged
Regulation shifted entirely to state accountancy boards

questions.explanation: Audit regulation shifted from self-regulation to independent government-mandated PCAOB oversight, prompted by scandals and SOX (2002).

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of Kinney's three 'constants'?

choices.text: The expectations gap
The regulatory environment
Determinants of information value
Organization of audit firms and contracts

questions.explanation: Kinney's three constants are determinants of information value, the expectations gap, and organization of audit firms/contracts. 'Regulatory environment' is a confirmed false distractor.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of Kinney's three 'trends'?

choices.text: The spirit of deregulation
Adoption of increasingly rigorous auditing standards
Development of information technology
Increased social importance of audited financial statements

questions.explanation: Kinney's three trends are deregulation, increased social importance of audited F/S (aka triumph of the corporation), and information technology. 'Rigorous standards adoption' is a distractor.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What is true of 'the expectations gap' relative to Kinney's trends?

choices.text: It reversed direction by 2002, due to SOX
It is not a trend at all, but one of Kinney's constants
It strengthened continuously after 2002
It only applies to private company audits

questions.explanation: The expectations gap is public unawareness of audit/GAAP limitations, causing 'where were the auditors?' after failures — it's a constant, not a trend.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: Which trend reversed direction by 2002 due to SOX?

choices.text: Triumph of the corporation
The spirit of deregulation
Information technology adoption
The determinants of information value

questions.explanation: The deregulation trend (1970s-2000s) reversed with SOX in 2002, which significantly re-regulated the profession by creating the PCAOB.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: How has technology impacted investors' use of information?

choices.text: It increased the cost of trading and slowed information delivery
It decreased the cost of information/trading and increased accessibility
It had no measurable effect on investors
It eliminated the need for financial disclosures entirely

questions.explanation: Technology decreased the cost of information/trading (online trading, no broker needed) and increased accessibility/timeliness (real-time disclosures vs. waiting for press releases).

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What does SOX Section 101 do?

choices.text: Establishes internal control requirements for issuers
Establishes the PCAOB as a nonprofit corporation to oversee public company audits
Requires CEO/CFO certification of financials
Bans specific non-audit services

questions.explanation: SOX Section 101 establishes the PCAOB itself as a nonprofit corporation to oversee public company audits.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What does SOX Section 102 require?

choices.text: Requires the PCAOB to inspect every audit annually
Requires public accounting firms auditing issuers to register with the PCAOB
Requires SEC approval of every audit report
Establishes criminal penalties for audit fraud

questions.explanation: Section 102 requires public accounting firms auditing issuers to register with the PCAOB before providing audit services.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What authority does SOX Section 103 give the PCAOB?

choices.text: Authority to prosecute securities fraud criminally
Authority to establish auditing, quality control, ethics, and independence standards
Authority to set GAAP for all public companies
Authority to appoint the SEC Chair

questions.explanation: Section 103 authorizes the PCAOB to establish auditing, quality control, ethics, and independence standards for registered public accounting firms.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What does SOX Section 104 establish?

choices.text: Auditing and independence standard-setting
Ongoing inspections of registered firms, frequency based on issuer count
Registration of public accounting firms
PCAOB funding via accounting support fees

questions.explanation: Section 104 requires the PCAOB to conduct ongoing inspections of registered firms, with frequency based on the number of issuers they audit.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What does SOX Section 109 establish?

choices.text: Foreign accounting firm registration requirements
PCAOB funding, primarily via mandatory accounting support fees on issuers
SEC oversight authority over the Board
Recognition of GAAP-setting bodies

questions.explanation: Section 109 establishes the PCAOB's funding, primarily via mandatory accounting support fees assessed on issuers based on relative market capitalization.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: Which statement about the PCAOB is NOT true?

choices.text: It sets audit and quality control standards
It is a United States government agency
It has 5 members
It inspects registered accounting firms

questions.explanation: The PCAOB is a private nonprofit corporation with a government mandate — explicitly not a US government agency, despite its regulatory role.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What is Generative AI (Gen-AI)?

choices.text: AI that runs exclusively on local, on-premise hardware
Cloud-based large language models that create content from user prompts
AI used only for image recognition
A rules-based system with no learning capability

questions.explanation: Gen-AI refers to cloud-based LLMs that create content from prompts; strong at unstructured data but with privacy risks and hallucinations.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What is the advantage of Edge AI over Generative AI?

choices.text: It incorporates more cutting-edge technology than Gen-AI
It better ensures data confidentiality and data sovereignty
It provides more complex analytical solutions
It is more efficient at drafting long-form text

questions.explanation: Edge AI's advantage is that it better ensures data confidentiality and data sovereignty by processing on local devices rather than the cloud.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What are example ways AI is currently used by auditors?

choices.text: Only replacing human judgment on materiality
Drafting memos, interpreting standards, contract analysis, and anomaly detection
Only scheduling client meetings
Only marketing and business development

questions.explanation: Cited examples include drafting workpapers/memos, interpreting standards, contract/lease analysis, disclosure checklist review, and anomaly/fraud detection.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What are key risks firms face in using Generative AI?

choices.text: AI in auditing carries no meaningful risks
Data privacy breaches, hallucinations, and bias/explainability concerns
Only higher software licensing costs
Only that clients might refuse AI use entirely

questions.explanation: Key risks: data privacy/security breaches, hallucinations (confidently wrong outputs), and bias/lack of explainability from 'black box' models.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: What are the actual arguments FOR dismantling the PCAOB?

choices.text: The PCAOB's authority is too limited to be effective
The SEC could accomplish the objectives more efficiently, and PCAOB rule-making goes too far
The PCAOB fails to accomplish its stated objectives
The PCAOB has no enforcement power at all

questions.explanation: Confirmed arguments for dismantling: the SEC could do it more efficiently, and PCAOB rule-making goes too far.

questions.module: Module 2: Regulatory History, SOX, and AI in Auditing
questions.prompt: How did the PCAOB avoid being shuttered in the 2025 budget reconciliation fight?

choices.text: Congress voted directly to preserve funding
A parliamentarian ruled the provision was a policy change under the Byrd rule, requiring 60 votes
The Supreme Court blocked the bill
The AICPA lobbied the provision out

questions.explanation: A Senate parliamentarian ruled the defunding provision was a policy change (not a budget matter) under the Byrd rule, requiring 60 votes it couldn't get.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: Conceptually, what is a 'standard'?

choices.text: A law passed by Congress governing a specific industry
A benchmark or agreed-upon criterion specifying required actions or quality levels
A voluntary suggestion with no enforcement mechanism
A price ceiling set by a regulatory body

questions.explanation: A standard is a benchmark or agreed-upon criterion specifying required (or presumptively required) actions/quality levels, creating consistency and a basis for evaluating performance.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: What distinguishes a 'profession' from an 'occupation'?

choices.text: A profession simply pays more than an occupation
Specialized knowledge plus self-regulation/autonomy over that knowledge
A profession requires a 4-year degree; an occupation does not
There is no meaningful distinction between the terms

questions.explanation: Specialized knowledge unavailable to non-members, combined with self-regulation/autonomy over that knowledge, is what distinguishes a profession from an occupation.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: Why do professions establish standards?

choices.text: Purely to increase billing rates for members
To serve the public good, signal quality, and preempt heavier government regulation
Because government agencies mandate it for every profession
To eliminate all competition from other professions

questions.explanation: Professions set standards to ensure knowledge serves the public good, signal quality assurance, and preempt heavier external/government regulation.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: What is 'legitimacy' in the context of standard-setting, and why does it matter?

choices.text: A legal certification issued by a government agency
A perception that an entity's actions are socially desirable and proper
A synonym for 'profitability' in the standard-setting context
A measure of how many firms comply with a given standard

questions.explanation: Legitimacy is a generalized perception that an entity's actions are socially desirable/proper; it matters because standard-setters have an inherent conflict of interest regulating their own profession.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: What are two approaches by which standard-setters obtain legitimacy?

choices.text: Litigation and lobbying
Representative inclusion of stakeholders, and expertise/rigorous due process
Advertising and public relations campaigns
Mandatory licensing exams for all members

questions.explanation: Representative legitimacy comes from including diverse stakeholders; expertise/due-process legitimacy comes from technical competence and a rigorous process.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off of the representative approach to legitimacy?

choices.text: It has no real cost — it is purely beneficial
Increased cost, slower process, and potential for watered-down standards
It eliminates the need for public comment periods
It automatically guarantees SEC approval

questions.explanation: The representative approach trades speed for buy-in — more stakeholders means higher coordination costs, a slower process, and potential compromise/watered-down standards.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: What three themes characterize codes of ethics, per Perliss et al.?

choices.text: Legal, illegal, and quasi-legal
Aspirational, educational, and regulatory
Federal, state, and local
Mandatory, optional, and voluntary

questions.explanation: Codes of ethics are aspirational (goals/ideals), educational (commentary/explanation), or regulatory (rules with enforcement) — most codes blend all three.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: What is a key criticism of self-regulation through codes of ethics?

choices.text: Codes are too strictly enforced, leaving no room for judgment
Codes can be self-serving window dressing/economic protectionism
Codes are always written by government regulators
Codes have never been shown to affect professional practice

questions.explanation: A key criticism is that self-regulating codes can be self-serving 'window dressing'/economic protectionism, promoting the profession's interests over the public's.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: What authority does SOX Section 103 give the PCAOB?

choices.text: Authority to prosecute securities fraud criminally
Authority to establish auditing, quality control, ethics, and independence standards
Authority to set GAAP for all public companies
Authority to appoint the SEC Chair

questions.explanation: SOX Section 103 authorizes the PCAOB to establish auditing, quality control, ethics, and independence standards for registered public accounting firms.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: What process does the PCAOB follow in developing new standards?

choices.text: A closed-door process with no external input
A notice-and-comment process seeking public comment on proposed standards
A direct congressional vote on every standard
A process relying solely on academic peer review

questions.explanation: The PCAOB follows a notice-and-comment process: seeking public comment on concept releases and proposed/re-proposed standards before finalizing them.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the PCAOB's four elements of economic impact analysis?

choices.text: The need for the new rule or standard
Prevailing costs of capital in the current environment
Reasonable alternatives to the proposed rule
The economic impact of the rule and its alternatives

questions.explanation: The PCAOB's four elements are the need for the rule, the baseline, alternatives considered, and the economic impact of the rule and alternatives. 'Prevailing costs of capital' is not one of them.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: Which statement about the ASB is NOT true?

choices.text: The ASB may issue audit, attest, or quality management standards
The ASB sets standards for auditors of non-issuers in the US
The ASB is responsible for inspecting auditors annually
The ASB has 19 members

questions.explanation: The ASB has 19 members (a quiz question flags '18' as a confirmed typo) and does NOT conduct annual inspections — that's a PCAOB function, not the ASB's.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: The PCAOB sets standards in every category EXCEPT which one?

choices.text: Quality control standards
Consulting standards
Ethics standards
Audit standards

questions.explanation: The PCAOB sets audit, quality control, and ethics/independence standards — it does NOT set 'consulting standards,' which falls outside its authority.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: Which statement about the IAASB is true?

choices.text: It is overseen by the SEC Practice Section
It is part of an umbrella organization called IFEA
It has 5 full-time members
Its standards have been directly adopted in the US

questions.explanation: The IAASB sits under the International Foundation for Ethics and Audit (IFEA) as of 2023, has 16 members, and its standards aren't directly adopted for US public company audits.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: What is the general convergence/divergence trend among the ASB, IAASB, and PCAOB?

choices.text: All three standard-setters use identical numbering and structure
ASB and IAASB converged via the Clarification Project; PCAOB diverges more
PCAOB and IAASB converged; ASB remains entirely separate
There has been no meaningful convergence effort among any of the three

questions.explanation: ASB and IAASB largely converged through the Clarification Project; PCAOB standards diverge more, especially regarding the auditor's report.

questions.module: Module 3: The Sources and Purposes of Professional Standards
questions.prompt: In auditing standards, what does the word 'should' signal?

choices.text: Unconditional — always required with no exceptions
Presumptively mandatory — required unless alternatives are shown sufficient
Purely optional, a matter of judgment
No formal meaning — stylistic word choice

questions.explanation: 'Should' signals a presumptively mandatory requirement — required unless the auditor demonstrates alternative actions were sufficient.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a requirement of an auditor identified by AS 1000?

choices.text: Independence and ethics
Patience
Due professional care
Competence

questions.explanation: AS 1000's three requirements are independence/ethics, due professional care, and competence. 'Patience' was a joke distractor confirming the real list.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: What is the overall purpose of auditing, per the 'division of responsibility' framing?

choices.text: To prepare the financial statements for management
To lend credibility to F/S that would otherwise be suspect due to conflicts of interest
To guarantee the company's future profitability
To replace internal accounting staff

questions.explanation: The auditor's role is to lend credibility to financial statements that would otherwise be suspect, given conflicts of interest inherent in the corporate structure.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: What does 'competence' mean under AS 1000, and how is it developed?

choices.text: Solely obtaining a CPA license
Training and proficiency built through education, licensure, and experience, maintained over time
Automatic once hired by an accounting firm
Only years of tenure, regardless of formal training

questions.explanation: Competence is having the training/proficiency needed, built through education, licensure, and practical experience, and must be maintained via continuing education.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: A newly licensed CPA claims she is now automatically competent under AS 1000. Is this appropriate?

choices.text: Appropriate — the CPA license is sufficient for all future engagements
Inappropriate — competence is engagement-specific and must be continually maintained
Appropriate, but only for the first five years post-licensure
Inappropriate — licensure has no bearing on competence at all

questions.explanation: Licensure is a baseline, not a guarantee of competence for every engagement; competence is engagement-specific and must be continually maintained.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: How does independence in fact differ from independence in appearance?

choices.text: They are the same concept described two different ways
In fact is the actual state of mind; in appearance is how a reasonable third party would view it
Only 'in fact' matters legally; 'in appearance' is just good practice
Only 'in appearance' is testable; 'in fact' can never be verified

questions.explanation: In fact = actual state of mind, unaffected by influences that compromise judgment. In appearance = avoidance of circumstances a reasonable, informed third party would view as compromising.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: Why do both independence in fact AND independence in appearance matter?

choices.text: In fact matters for legal liability only; appearance has no real-world importance
In fact is the substance enabling an unbiased opinion; in appearance sustains public trust even absent actual bias
Neither actually matters if the audit opinion is ultimately correct
Appearance matters only for public companies, not private ones

questions.explanation: In-fact independence is the substance that lets the auditor's opinion be genuinely unbiased; in-appearance independence matters because public trust in audited F/S depends on perceived independence.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: A speaker tells high schoolers that independence just means avoiding financial interests in a client. Is this correct?

choices.text: Correct — independence is entirely about financial interests
Incorrect — SEC rules also cover employment, business relationships, non-audit services, and contingent fees
Correct, but only for engagement partners specifically
Incorrect — SEC rules only cover appearance, not financial interests at all

questions.explanation: Financial-interest rules are only one category; SEC rules also cover employment relationships, business relationships, non-audit services, and contingent fees.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: What is due professional care?

choices.text: Simply completing all required checklists regardless of quality
Exercising the skill/diligence of a reasonably prudent, competent auditor, with critical review of work
Following management's instructions on how to conduct the audit
A purely subjective standard with no defined benchmark

questions.explanation: Due professional care is exercising the skill/diligence of a reasonably prudent, competent auditor — careful performance and critical review of work at every level.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: Professional skepticism involves a critical assessment of which of these specifically?

choices.text: The financial statements as a whole
Audit evidence
Internal controls over financial reporting only
Management's general trustworthiness

questions.explanation: Professional skepticism involves a critical assessment specifically of audit evidence — not the F/S generally, ICFR alone, or management's trustworthiness as people.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: A manager advises new staff to always view management as dishonest to maintain skepticism. Is this appropriate?

choices.text: Appropriate — assuming dishonesty is the safest form of skepticism
Inappropriate — the standard is a neutral, evidence-driven mindset, not assumed dishonesty
Appropriate, but only for public company audits
Inappropriate — auditors should generally trust management by default

questions.explanation: AU-C 200 says the auditor should neither assume dishonesty nor unquestioned honesty — skepticism is a neutral, evidence-driven questioning mindset, not a presumption of guilt.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: What did EY actually do in the Sealed Air independence case?

choices.text: EY hired the client's former controller into a senior role
EY solicited confidential RFP and audit committee information from the client's CAO
EY held a direct financial interest in the client's stock
EY provided prohibited bookkeeping services to the client

questions.explanation: EY solicited and received confidential competitive intelligence and confidential audit committee information from Sealed Air's then-CAO during the RFP process.

questions.module: Module 4: The Qualities of the Auditor (Competence, Independence, Due Care)
questions.prompt: Which independence standard did the Sealed Air conduct actually violate?

choices.text: The specific $10,000 credit card balance threshold
The general 'reasonable investor' appearance-of-independence standard
The direct financial interest prohibition
The mandatory partner rotation requirement
